fixes.explanation: Son it is, friend. Ziba, a servant of Saul's house, says, “There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet.” (2 Samuel 9:3). He doesn't give the son's name yet, only that he's Jonathan's son.

Hebron isn't mentioned here, friend. David asks, “Where is he?” and Ziba answers, “Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.” (2 Samuel 9:4). Lo-debar is the place, and Machir is the man whose house it is. I'd have grabbed the famous-sounding town too, and I'd have been just as wrong.

Bethlehem doesn't come up in this passage, friend. David asks, “Where is he?” and Ziba says, “Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.” (2 Samuel 9:4). Bethlehem is the first town that jumps to my mind too, and my mind has been wrong before.

Standing up, like a handshake at the door? Not here, friend. The text says Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, “…fell facedown in reverence.” (2 Samuel 9:6). He goes low, and the verse says it was reverence.

No gift in this scene, friend. The text says Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, “…fell facedown in reverence.” (2 Samuel 9:6). The verse mentions no gift, only that he went facedown. Reverence is how he comes in.

Right, friend. David says, “Do not be afraid…” and then he gives his reason: “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan.” (2 Samuel 9:7). Mephibosheth is facedown, and David has already called his name. Then comes the king's calm word that he doesn't need to be afraid.
Army isn't in the promise, friend. David says, “I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul…” (2 Samuel 9:7). It's land, plain old land. Saul's land goes back to Saul's grandson.
That's a smaller offer than the real one, friend. David says, “…you will always eat at my table.” (2 Samuel 9:7). David says always, and he never mentions feast days. The real offer is bigger.

Soldiers aren't in the comparison, friend. The text says, “So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table like one of the king’s own sons.” (2 Samuel 9:11). The verse compares how he eats to a son of the king. It picks sons, not soldiers.

Servants is right, friend. The text says, “…all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants of Mephibosheth.” (2 Samuel 9:12). Mephibosheth also has a young son named Mica. The man who called himself a servant now has servants of his own.

True, friend. The text says, “So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table…” (2 Samuel 9:13). The verse gives the reason too, the king's table. Before this he was in Lo-debar, and now he lives in Jerusalem.
